title: Dependability Alpha: Cross-Functional Retro + Action Log
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc captures the retro from the Dependability Alpha pilot (Jan-Feb 2026), decisions made across teams, and the consolidated action log for the next quarter. The goal was to validate cross-functional processes for establishing service-level objectives (SLOs), iterate on measurement pipelines, and stress our fallback policies during a controlled traffic experiment. This is intentionally pragmatic — notes to self and stakeholders; not a final playbook.

What we ran (quick summary):
- Pilot name: Dependability Alpha (external name later: Dependability Pilot)
- Services in scope: API Gateway, TextGen Router, KV cache service, Tokenizer microservice
- SLO types tested: availability (p99 error rate), latency (p95 tail), correctness (regression rate on eval set)
- Duration: 2026-01-10 to 2026-02-28
- Traffic profiles: normal baseline + two injected spike windows (one regional, one global)

Highlights / Wins:
- Observability: infra team shipped the lightweight SLO exporter (slo-exporter v0.3) that normalized error budgets across services — allowed cross-service dashboards within 48h of deployment.
- Rollback cadence: Canary->50%->100% worked end-to-end; automatic fallback to cheaper model variant activated correctly under GPU shortage scenario.
- Cross-team coordination: Daily 20-minute syncs reduced notification storm; on-call rotation stubbed into the experiment schedule with clearly identified owners.

Pain points and root causes (brief):
1) Measurement drift: Tokenizer reports different error taxonomy from TextGen Router. Root cause: inconsistent error codes and missing semantic mapping in slo-exporter. Concrete consequence: mismatched incident triggers between teams.
2) Alert fatigue: Too many alerts during spike windows; paging rules fired for transient cache thrashing. Root cause: thresholds were too tight and not aligned with bursty traffic shape.
3) Ownership gaps: Nobody owned the end-to-end correctness SLO (model output regression) — observability pipeline produced the signal but there was no decision owner for remediation.
4) Capacity planning mismatch: Dedicated capacity autoscale thresholds didn't take pipeline cold-starts into account leading to short-lived errors during ramp.

Key decisions made during retro:
- Adopt a simple canonical error taxonomy across services (see action 1). All teams must map local errors to this taxonomy before emitting to slo-exporter.
- Introduce an explicit "SLO steward" role per product area responsible for signal verification, runbook updates, and quarterly SLO reviews.
- Adjust alerting windows: increase burst-tolerant cooldowns for cache-related metrics and add a circuit-breaker style suppression for spikes lasting < 30s.
- For correctness SLOs, require an owner in Product-ML to sign off on remediation playbooks before the next pilot.

Action log (priority, owner, ETA):
- ACTION 1: Create canonical error mapping spec + translation table for slo-exporter. Owner: Ravi Patel (infra). ETA: 2026-03-20. Linked: JIRA-REL-421.
- ACTION 2: Define SLO steward role template and list of responsibilities; assign stewards for API Gateway, TextGen Router, and KV Cache. Owner: Maya Chen (SRE lead) & Priya Nair (product). ETA: 2026-03-12.
- ACTION 3: Add correctness SLO owner requirement to service launch checklist. Owner: Sofia Alvarez (platform-eng). ETA: 2026-03-05.
- ACTION 4: Tune alert cooldowns and add suppression for cache thrash spikes < 30s (experimental rule set). Owner: Jordan Brooks (observability). ETA: 2026-03-18.
- ACTION 5: Update autoscale policy to account for cold-start windows (add warm-up buffer + predictive scale-out). Owner: Ethan Li (platform infra). ETA: 2026-03-25.
- ACTION 6: Draft cross-functional runbook for model-fallback including telemetry checks and customer-impact communications template. Owner: Priya Nair (product-ml). ETA: 2026-03-22.
- ACTION 7: Run a focused tabletop exercise around the correctness SLO failure scenario; invite CS, Product, Legal for communications practice. Owner: Maya Chen. ETA: 2026-04-02.

Implementation notes and templates to reuse:
- Error taxonomy: class -> transient|permanent|client_error|server_error; map to numerical codes for exporter (0..99). Keep mapping doc as living Confluence page; short-term implementers can use a middleware shim to translate local codes to canonical codes.
- SLO steward checklist (minimum): 1) Validate signal integrity weekly; 2) Maintain owner's runbook; 3) Sign off on SLO changes; 4) Coordinate post-incident reviews.
- Runbook minimal sections: detection signal -> validation steps (manual quick-checks) -> mitigation steps -> public comms draft -> post-incident metrics to evaluate.

Metrics to track going into next pilot (targets are draft):
- SLO signal latency: time between event and metric ingestion < 60s (goal 30s).
- Correctness regression detection window: detect model-regression within 1 hour of deployment.
- Error taxonomy coverage: 100% services mapped by next release.
- Alert-to-action time: Median time from alert firing to first remediation step < 5 minutes for P1s.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Dependence on slo-exporter v0.3 stability. Mitigation: run exporter in high-availability mode and add local buffering for 72h on telemetry.
- Risk: Cross-team bandwidth — many action owners are stretched. Mitigation: prioritize top-3 actions (error taxonomy, SLO stewards, correctness ownership) and defer lower-risk items.
- Risk: Customer communications cadence unclear for correctness regressions. Mitigation: pre-author templates and legal sign-off on worst-case language.

Communications and governance:
- Weekly status: SLO steward sync (30m) — focus on signal health and outstanding action items. Invite: SRE, Product, Observability, Platform.
- Monthly review: Exec summary for Reliability Council; include error budget burn, high-level mitigations, and any required capacity commitments.
- Escalation: If correctness SLO breaches and rollback fails, trigger the Incident Response + Product Exec on-call (per existing incident policy).

Next pilot changes (operational checklist):
1) All services publish canonical error codes via the translation shim.
2) Stewards assigned and first steward sync scheduled.
3) Alert cooldowns updated per experimental rule set.
4) Canary policy updated to include correctness regression holdback (auto-stop canary on regression > threshold).

Open questions (to resolve before next pilot):
- How tight should "detect within 1 hour" be for correctness SLOs given model evaluation costs? (Product-ML input needed)
- Acceptable error budget burn for cache-layer transient spikes during a major marketing event? (GTM and infra alignment required)
- Who approves increased retention for telemetry (cost impact)? (Finance + Observability)

Appendix: notes-to-self / raw snippets from debriefs:
- "We got too clever with alert rules; simpler threshold + suppression worked better."
- "Stewards reduce last-mile ambiguity; having at least one person who can say 'this is the correct signal' is huge."
- "Model fallback needs a clear customer-impact mapping (0: no visible impact -> 3: degraded responses); attach this to runbook steps."

Immediate next steps (this week):
- Ravi to drop initial mapping spec in Confluence and ping teams.
- Maya to send steward assignment calendar invites and template checklist.
- Jordan to prototype cooldown config and run it in staging.

If you're reviewing: please add comments inline in Confluence page linked above or raise JIRA tasks against the REL epic. This doc will be updated iteratively and folded into the broader Dependability program playbook after the next pilot cycle.

Last updated by: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) on 2026-03-10
summary: Retro and concrete action plan from the Dependability Alpha pilot. Focus areas: canonical error taxonomy, SLO steward role, alert tuning, autoscale warm-up, correctness SLO ownership, and communications templates.
